description.summary: A cross-cultural class of supernatural beings, generally malevolent or morally ambivalent, found in nearly every major religious and folkloric tradition. The Christian-Islamic concept of demons as evil spirits or fallen angels developed from older Greek, Hebrew, Mesopotamian, and Zoroastrian categories of intermediate spirits.
description.full: A demon is, broadly, a supernatural being whose function in a religious or folkloric system is to harm, tempt, or oppose humans, the divine order, or both. The English word descends from Greek δαίμων (daimōn), originally a morally neutral term for an intermediate divine being between gods and humans, used by Hesiod, Plato, and the Pre-Socratics. Hellenistic and early Christian writers narrowed the term to malevolent spirits, conflating it with Hebrew shedim and se'irim and with the fallen-angel traditions of Second-Temple Jewish apocalyptic literature (1 Enoch, Jubilees). Christian theologians (Augustine of Hippo, Aquinas) systematised demons as fallen angels under Lucifer/Satan; medieval and Renaissance demonology produced extensive hierarchies (Pseudomonarchia Daemonum, 1577; Lesser Key of Solomon, 17th century) and lists of named demons (Asmodeus, Belial, Beelzebub, Astaroth, Belphegor). Islamic tradition distinguishes shayāṭīn (devils, with Iblīs as their head) from jinn (a separate created order with free will, capable of being good or evil). Zoroastrianism inverts the older Indo-Iranian deva/asura distinction so that the daēvas become demons under Angra Mainyu. Hindu cosmology recognises asuras and rākshasas, and Buddhism the māras and naraka-beings, but in both traditions such beings are subject to karma and rebirth rather than being eternally damned. Folkloric demons appear in Mesopotamian texts (utukku, Lamaštu, Pazuzu), in Japanese tradition (oni, yōkai), and across many other cultures.

etymology.origin: Greek δαίμων (daimōn), of disputed root: possibly from δαίεσθαι 'to divide, distribute', i.e. 'distributor of fates'. The Latin daemon was theologically narrowed to evil spirits in patristic and medieval Christian usage.
etymology.meaning: In classical Greek, an intermediate divine being or guardian spirit; in later Christian theology, an evil supernatural being or fallen angel.
etymology.first_use: Greek daimōn attested in Homer (8th century BCE) and Hesiod; the narrow 'evil-spirit' sense crystallises in Greek-Jewish and Christian texts of the Hellenistic and early imperial periods.

coloration: red, black, or pale skin in Christian iconography
blue or green in some Eastern traditions

features.description: Common in Christian iconography from the early Middle Ages onward, drawing on classical satyr/Pan imagery and biblical descriptions of cherubim
Composite forms, e.g. Pazuzu (Mesopotamian) with lion's body and bird's wings; oni with horns and tiger-skin loincloths
Many traditions hold demons to be primarily incorporeal beings able to assume bodies

physical.morphology: Highly variable: from invisible spirits to gigantic monstrous bodies; the form depends on the tradition.

abilities.description: Inhabiting a human body and overriding the will of the host; central to Christian and Islamic traditions and addressed by exorcism
Inducing humans to sin or moral failure (Christianity, Islam, Buddhism's Mara)
Across many traditions, demons are held responsible for illness, accident, and ill-fortune
Especially in Islamic, Jewish, and Eastern traditions

patterns: Operate covertly through temptation, dreams, illness, or possession
Manifest visibly only in moments of crisis (exorcism, mystical encounter)
Are organised hierarchically in many medieval Christian and Islamic traditions

range.description: Demonology is a near-universal feature of human religious systems, with major systematised traditions in West Asia, Europe, North Africa, South and East Asia.

first_recorded.source: Sumerian and Akkadian incantation texts naming demonic beings (utukku, Lamaštu)

peak_activity_periods.description: Crystallisation of Christian and Rabbinic demonology
Medieval and early-modern European demonology, witch-hunts, and grimoire literature
Renewed Western popular fascination from The Exorcist (1973) onward

origins.cultural_roots: Pre-Axial-Age West Asian, Egyptian, and Indo-Iranian religious systems gave rise to demonological categories that were extensively reworked in the Hellenistic, Roman, and early Christian/Islamic periods.
origins.earliest_accounts: Sumerian and Akkadian incantation literature (e.g. the Maqlû series, the Lamaštu incantations); Egyptian Coffin Texts and Book of the Dead; the Avesta; the Hebrew Bible; the apocryphal 1 Enoch.
origins.folklore_connections: Local folkloric demonologies (oni, yōkai, ifrit, ghul, dybbuk, krasue, etc.) draw on and reshape these literate traditions and on indigenous spirit-beliefs.

timeline.event: Mesopotamian demonological literature: utukku, gallu, Lamaštu, Pazuzu in Sumerian and Akkadian incantations
Zoroastrian Gathas and later Avestan literature relegate the daēvas to demonic status
1 Enoch and Jubilees (3rd–2nd centuries BCE) develop the fallen-angel tradition (Watchers)
timeline.significance: Bridge between Hebrew Bible and later Christian/Islamic demonology

timeline.event: Augustine of Hippo's De Civitate Dei integrates Greek daimones into Christian demonology
timeline.significance: Shapes Latin Christian demonology for a millennium

timeline.event: Thomas Aquinas systematises Catholic angelology and demonology in the Summa Theologiae
Heinrich Kramer's Malleus Maleficarum (1486) institutionalises the witchcraft–demonology connection
Johann Weyer publishes Pseudomonarchia Daemonum (appended to De Praestigiis Daemonum)
Roman Catholic Rituale Romanum (1614) standardises the rite of exorcism
William Friedkin's The Exorcist (Warner Bros.) opens in U.S. cinemas
timeline.significance: Reignites Western popular interest in demonology and exorcism

timeline.event: Vatican issues revised rite of exorcism (De Exorcismis et Supplicationibus Quibusdam)

history.modern_era: In the present day, belief in demons remains widespread among adherents of Christianity, Islam, and many other religions. The Catholic Church maintains an official ministry of exorcism, with associations such as the International Association of Exorcists (founded 1990, recognised by the Holy See in 2014). Academic study of demons proceeds in religious-studies, anthropology, and history-of-religion departments worldwide.

documentary.name: 1 Enoch (Book of Enoch)
documentary.description: Second-Temple Jewish apocalyptic text developing the Watchers / fallen-angel tradition that underlies later Jewish, Christian, and Islamic demonologies.
documentary.analysis: Foundational pseudepigraphic source for fallen-angel traditions.
documentary.source: Nickelsburg, G. W. E. (2001), 1 Enoch: A Commentary

documentary.name: Malleus Maleficarum
documentary.description: Heinrich Kramer's manual on the prosecution of witches, deeply integrating demonology with witch-hunting.
documentary.analysis: Highly influential and widely-criticised early-modern demonological work.

documentary.name: Pseudomonarchia Daemonum
documentary.description: Johann Weyer's catalogue of named demons, appended to De Praestigiis Daemonum.

paranormal.name: Real spiritual beings
paranormal.description: In Christian, Islamic, Jewish, and many other religious systems, demons are understood as real spiritual beings, ontologically distinct from humans and angels, who oppose the divine order.
proponents: Major Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, and Islamic theologians

paranormal.name: Fallen-angel doctrine
paranormal.description: Christian and post-Quranic Islamic traditions hold that demons are angels who rebelled against God under a leader (Satan / Iblīs).

skeptical.name: Cultural and psychological framing
skeptical.description: Demonological phenomena (possession, attack, oppression) are interpreted by anthropologists and clinicians as a religiously-coded language for psychological, neurological, and social distress.
evidence_cited: Diagnostic overlap with dissociative and psychotic disorders

skeptical.name: Comparative-religion perspective
skeptical.description: 'Demons' are a comparative category that obscures the very different conceptions of harmful spiritual beings across cultures (asuras, jinn, oni, etc.); careful religious-studies work prefers tradition-specific terminology.

traditions: Islamic demonology and the jinn-shayāṭīn distinction
stories: Solomon and the demons (Testament of Solomon)
Mara's assault on the Buddha (Pali Canon)
Iblis' refusal to bow to Adam (Quran)
folklore.beliefs: Belief in demons remains widespread across Christianity, Islam, and many other faiths. Practical responses include prayer, sacramentals, exorcism, ruqyah, mantra, talismans, and other apotropaic practices.

literature: The Screwtape Letters — C. S. Lewis (1942)
music: Symphonie fantastique, mvt 5 'Songe d'une nuit de sabbat' — Berlioz (1830)
other: Modern Catholic and Pentecostal exorcism ministries
